title: Ethical Concepts, Ethical Theories, Professional Code of Conduct and Midwifery Dilemmas
introduction: Ethics examines moral conduct and safeguards clients against the abuse of power inherent in the caregiver-client relationship. Navigating complex maternal-child dilemmas—from assisted reproduction and selective reduction to treatment refusal—requires mastering ethical theories, seven core bioethical principles, the NMCN Code of Professional Conduct, and the ten-step Ethical Decision-Making Model.
learningOutcomes: 4.1 Define ethics, distinguish ethics from law, and differentiate personal ethics, professional ethics, nursing ethics, and bioethics.
4.2 Compare teleological (utilitarian), deontological (rule-based), and caring ethical theories, and define the seven core ethical principles in health care.
4.3 Trace the transition from the 1893 Florence Nightingale Pledge to modern codes and explain the NMCN Code of Professional Conduct regarding consumers, colleagues, the public, and global health.
4.4 Analyze major ethical dilemmas in midwifery and perinatal care, including assisted reproduction, abortion, selective reduction, intrauterine fetal treatment, HIV disclosure, and consent refusal.
4.5 Apply the ten-step Model for Ethical Decision Making to resolve competing ethical values rationally and defensibly.

content.heading: Ethics vs. Law and Types of Ethics
content.body: Ethics is a method of inquiry into human morality, the formal or informal standards governing right conduct in a group, and a safeguard against abuse of power in the inherently unequal client-caregiver relationship. Articles 1A and 1B of the ICM International Code of Ethics for Midwives (1993) frame midwifery as an equal partnership respecting each woman's informed choice and active participation. While some equate ethics and morals, others distinguish ethics (publicly stated formal rules/values) from morals (personally committed principles). Ethics differs sharply from law: laws are formal, written rules enforceable by government with mandatory welfare duties and legal punishments, controlled externally; ethics consists of internal moral principles ('rules people ought to obey') informing laws, carrying no legal punishments (though professional violations may bring suspension or dismissal) and always demanding standards equal to or higher than the law. Once a client willingly submits to care, a legal contract of care arises. Ethics is categorized into Personal ethics (values acquired across life via family, religion, education, and peers—'ought to do' vs. 'ought not to do'), Professional ethics (unwritten informal and written formal codes peculiar to a profession), Nursing ethics (protecting clients in nursing), and Bioethics (ethics applied to human life and health).

content.heading: Ethical Theories and Seven Core Ethical Principles
content.body: Clinical ethics draws on three foundational theories: (1) Teleological (Consequentialist / Utilitarian) Theory—judges rightness solely by probable outcomes or utility ('greatest good or least harm for the greatest number', exemplified by cost-benefit health policies); (2) Deontological (Rule-Based) Theory—grounds morality in inherent duty and moral obligation independent of consequences (e.g., a deontologist insists on strict truth-telling always, whereas a utilitarian might withhold truth if it causes greater harm); and (3) Relationship-Based or Caring Theory. Flowing largely from deontological frameworks are seven guiding ethical principles that help nurses weigh risks against benefits: (1) Autonomy—respect for persons, personal liberty, and self-determination; (2) Nonmaleficence—the 'no harm' principle of avoiding injury and risk of harm; (3) Beneficence—the duty to do good and act in the client's best interest; (4) Justice—fairness and equal opportunity, giving each person what is due (e.g., never discriminating against a disabled mother); (5) Fidelity—promise keeping; (6) Veracity—truth telling essential to trust; and (7) Accountability—completing work satisfactorily, accepting consequences, and being answerable for actions.

content.heading: From the 1893 Nightingale Pledge to the NMCN Code of Professional Conduct
content.body: Formal nursing ethical codes began in the 19th century with religious orders and the secular Florence Nightingale Pledge of 1893 (modelled on the Hippocratic Oath, pledging purity, abstaining from harmful drugs, confidentiality, and loyal aid to physicians). Because its acquiescent tone no longer suited 21st-century autonomous nursing, it was replaced by the modern Nurses' Pledge. The NMCN Code of Professional Conduct places the client at the centre of care to inform nurses of their required accountability and inform the public, employers, and other professions of expected standards. Toward the Health Care Consumer, the nurse must: provide care without prejudice (age, religion, ethnicity, race, nationality, gender, politics, health, or SES); uphold constitutional human rights; obtain informed consent from clients aged ≥18 (or parents/next of kin for minors); keep records confidential except for team consultation, court order, or public protection; avoid negligence, malpractice, and assault; maintain strictly professional relations and refuse bribes/preferential gifts; honour culture and beliefs; deliver accurate, comprehensible information while respecting those who decline information; respect client autonomy even if refusal risks harm or death to client or foetus unless overruled by court order; presume legal competence unless professionally assessed otherwise; apply equal consent principles to mentally ill clients (knowing statutory Mental Health Act safeguards); and give emergency life-preserving care without consent when clients cannot consent and care is in their best interest.

content.heading: Professional Duties to Colleagues, the Public, and Global Health
content.body: With Professional Colleagues, the nurse must collaborate strictly on ethical procedures; display 'esprit de corps' except in fraudulent or unethical practices; delegate and supervise subordinates according to competence; never ridicule colleagues (especially in front of clients or team members); accept personal accountability for actions and omissions regardless of directives from other professionals; be punctual and physically hand over patients and equipment; switch off mobile phones during patient care and classroom teaching; avoid using oneself in commercial product promotion or illicit trades such as hard-drug trafficking; reject undue gifts or gratifications; and ensure scientific technology aligns with patient safety, dignity, and rights. Toward the Public, the nurse protects society against harmful agents, considers physical/psychological/social care environments, assesses resource adequacy while reporting unsafe conditions to authorities, and contributes to policy making. Toward Global Health Organizations, the nurse implements international initiatives signed by Nigeria, NMCN, and NANNM and participates actively in national and international conferences.

content.heading: Ethical Issues and Dilemmas in Midwifery Practice
content.body: An ethical dilemma arises when equally compelling ethical reasons exist both for and against a course of action, requiring deliberate choice amidst competing personal and institutional values. Major maternal-child ethical dilemmas include: (1) Assisted Reproduction (artificial insemination, IVF and embryo transfer, surrogate parenthood)—expensive, rarely insured, with limited success, raising questions over a donor-conceived child's right to know their biological father and legal parental rights in surrogacy; (2) Abortion—pitting a woman's right to choose, privacy, and bodily autonomy against the belief that the foetus is a human being from conception deserving protection (a debate extending to post-fertilization contraceptives); (3) Selective Reduction in multifetal pregnancies caused by ovulation induction or IVF—terminating one or more fetuses so others can survive, intensified because the pregnancy was deeply desired; (4) Intrauterine Treatment of Fetal Conditions—experimental fetal surgery raising conflicts between maternal vs. fetal rights and consent, paralleling situations where a labouring mother refuses a caesarean section clearly needed for the foetus; and (5) additional dilemmas such as HIV/AIDS disclosure, withdrawal of life support, and refusal of consent for caesarean section or blood transfusion.

content.heading: Ten-Step Model for Ethical Decision Making
content.body: To resolve clinical dilemmas rationally rather than impulsively, nurses follow a ten-step Ethical Decision-Making Model: (1) Statement of the Problem—clearly, concisely state and validate the issue; (2) Value Clarification—examine personal and corporate belief systems and expected moral conduct; (3) Data Gathering—collect all clinical, social, and contributory facts; (4) Identification of the Ethical Problem—pinpoint which specific ethical principles are in conflict; (5) Identification of Decision Makers and Involved Parties—identify all stakeholders and define their roles; (6) Determination of Courses of Action—list potential options (choosing the most good or least harm if none are ideal); (7) Application of Ethical Principles for Resolution—weigh each option's benefits and risks against ethical principles to maximize benefit and minimize risk; (8) Reaching a Resolution—select a rational, feasible, defensible, and beneficial plan; (9) Resolution Implementation—specify what will be done, by whom, and under what conditions, then execute; and (10) Feedback/Outcome Evaluation—assess whether goals were met, who benefited and at what cost, and whether revision is needed (accepting a just, harm-reducing, beneficent outcome with some autonomy when no perfect solution exists).

inTextQuestions.question: How would a deontologist and a utilitarian differ regarding whether to tell a patient a distressing truth?
inTextQuestions.answer: A deontologist insists truth-telling is a moral duty that must never be violated regardless of consequences, whereas a utilitarian may argue truth-telling should be avoided if it will produce more harm than good.

inTextQuestions.question: Under the NMCN Code of Professional Conduct, when may a nurse legally provide care without a client's consent?
inTextQuestions.answer: In life-threatening emergencies when treatment is necessary to preserve life and the client is unable to consent (acting in their best interest), or when a client is lawfully detained under statutory powers (e.g., Mental Health Act) following proper safeguards.

inTextQuestions.question: Which ethical principle specifically requires fairness and equal opportunity—such as ensuring a disabled mother is not discriminated against?
Why is selective reduction in a multifetal pregnancy considered uniquely complex ethically?
inTextQuestions.answer: It involves the same moral conflicts as abortion (terminating one or more fetuses so others can survive outside the uterus), complicated further because the pregnancy involves long-awaited, deeply desired children.

saqs.question: Distinguish clearly between law and ethics across four key criteria, and differentiate personal ethics from professional ethics.
saqs.answer: Law consists of formal, written rules enforced externally by government with mandatory duties and legal punishments, whereas ethics consists of internal moral principles governing conscience with no statutory legal punishment (though professional codes always equal or exceed legal standards). Personal ethics are individual moral values acquired across life via family, religion, and peers, whereas professional ethics are formal (written codes) and informal moral responsibilities unique to a profession and monitored by peers.

saqs.question: Compare Teleological (Utilitarian) Theory and Deontological Theory, and define any five of the seven core health care ethical principles.
saqs.answer: Teleological/utilitarian theory judges an action's rightness solely by its outcomes ('greatest good or least harm for the greatest number'), whereas deontological theory judges the action itself by moral duty independent of consequences. Five core principles are: Autonomy (self-determination), Nonmaleficence (doing no harm), Beneficence (duty to do good), Justice (fairness and equal opportunity), and Fidelity (promise keeping) [others: Veracity and Accountability].

saqs.question: Outline the nurse's key ethical obligations toward the public and toward professional colleagues under the NMCN Code of Professional Conduct.
saqs.answer: Toward the public, the nurse protects society from harmful agents, considers the care environment's physical/psychological/social effects, reports inadequate resources or unsafe conditions to authorities, and contributes to policy making. Toward colleagues, the nurse collaborates only on ethical procedures, shows esprit de corps except in fraud/unethical practice, delegates safely by competence, never ridicules colleagues, remains personally accountable, hands over patients/equipment physically, switches off phones during care/teaching, and rejects undue gifts.

saqs.question: Discuss three prenatal or midwifery situations that create ethical dilemmas for nurses and explain the core moral tension in each.
saqs.answer: 1. Assisted reproduction (IVF, donor insemination, surrogacy): raises questions of high cost, limited access, the child's right to know a biological sperm donor, and parental rights in surrogacy. 2. Abortion: pits a woman's autonomy and right to privacy against the belief in fetal personhood from conception. 3. Intrauterine fetal treatment / C-section refusal: creates tension between maternal autonomy/consent and fetal rights or best medical interest.

saqs.question: List the ten sequential steps of the Model for Ethical Decision Making.
saqs.answer: 1. Statement of the problem; 2. Value clarification; 3. Data gathering; 4. Identification of the ethical problem; 5. Identification of decision makers and involved parties; 6. Determination of courses of action; 7. Application of ethical principles for resolution; 8. Reaching a resolution; 9. Resolution implementation; and 10. Feedback/outcome evaluation.
